Case File

Jacob Hope: A Name for the Round Lake Beach Baby — How Genetic Genealogy Reopened a 2001 Cold Case

The short version

The newborn boy the community named “Jacob Hope” was found dead on August 26, 2001, in a bag in a dumpster behind a grocery store on Rollins Road in Round Lake Beach, Illinois. The case went cold for more than two decades. After Round Lake Beach police reopened it in early 2024 and submitted the child’s DNA for genetic genealogy testing, investigators identified his biological parents.

On July 14, 2026, the Round Lake Beach Police Department and the Lake County State’s Attorney’s Office announced that Jennifer Lebron, 48, the child’s mother, was charged with two counts of involuntary manslaughter — not murder. She appeared in Lake County court on July 15, 2026, was released pending trial, and is scheduled to return to court on August 12, 2026.

Jennifer Lebron has been charged, not convicted. Under the law she is presumed innocent unless and until proven guilty in a court of law. The baby’s father, identified through the same investigation, is not suspected of any wrongdoing.

Case status: Charges filed July 14, 2026 · Court-active · Next hearing August 12, 2026 · No conviction.

New development (July 2026): a charge in Jacob Hope’s case

For nearly 25 years, the child had a name the community gave him but no name of his own on the record, and no one held to account. That changed in July 2026.

On July 14, 2026, the Round Lake Beach Police Department and the Lake County State’s Attorney’s Office announced in a joint statement that Jennifer Lebron, 48, of Lake Villa, had been charged in connection with the infant’s death. Authorities identify Lebron as the baby’s mother.

The precise charge matters, and we state it precisely: Lebron was charged with two counts of involuntary manslaughter. This is not a murder charge. In 2001, a different woman had been charged with first-degree murder in the case, but investigators later determined she had never been pregnant; those charges were dismissed in October 2001, and the case went cold.

Lebron appeared before Lake County Judge Rhonda K. Bruno on July 15, 2026. Prosecutors did not seek to detain her; the judge imposed a curfew and barred her from using drugs or alcohol while awaiting trial, and she was released. She is scheduled to return to court on August 12, 2026.

A charge is an accusation, not a verdict. Jennifer Lebron is presumed innocent unless and until she is convicted in a court of law. We will update this file as the case proceeds. Whether Ms. Lebron has retained an attorney was not stated in available reporting.

For nearly a quarter century he had no name. A newborn boy, found in the late summer of 2001 in Round Lake Beach, Illinois, and carried through the years only as a case number. The people who could not forget him gave him one: Jacob Hope — a name chosen by child-welfare advocates at AMT Children of Hope so that a child who was never legally named in life would not be nameless in memory.

This is the story of how a 2001 cold case was reopened — and how the same forensic science now solving decades-old identifications gave investigators a path back to Jacob's family. It is a story about a method, and about the care that method demands. A charge is not a conviction, and everyone named here is presumed innocent unless a court says otherwise.

What is alleged — stated precisely

In July 2026, the Lake County (Illinois) State's Attorney's Office approved two counts of involuntary manslaughter against Jennifer Lebron, 48, whom investigators identify as Jacob's mother. She was arrested on the morning of July 14, 2026, and was due for a first court appearance the following day.

A few points matter, and they matter exactly as written:

  • The charges are two counts of involuntary manslaughter — a felony. They are not murder charges.
  • Ms. Lebron has been charged, not convicted. These are allegations that have not been tested in court. She is presumed innocent.
  • The infant's father was also identified through the investigation but, according to the reporting, is not believed to be criminally involved and has not been charged.

Timeline

  • August 26, 2001 — A newborn boy is found deceased, in a bag in a dumpster behind a grocery store on Rollins Road in Round Lake Beach. He carries no legal name. The Lake County Major Crimes Task Force opens the investigation.
  • September 2001 — A woman is charged with first-degree murder in connection with the case. Those charges are later dropped. Her name is not part of the public record. (This thread matters — more below.)
  • Early 2024 — The case is reopened. The child's DNA is submitted for investigative genetic genealogy (IGG) testing.
  • 2024–2026 — The genealogy work returns a match to a relative of the infant's father. Traditional genealogy and follow-up build outward from that relative to identify both parents.
  • July 14, 2026 — Jennifer Lebron is arrested and charged with two counts of involuntary manslaughter; she is due in court July 15, 2026. The father is identified but not charged.

The science: what actually cracked the case

Investigative genetic genealogy did not "solve" this case by itself, and it did not point a finger at a person. It pointed at a family — and then people did the rest.

Here is the shape of it. A dense DNA profile is built from the case sample and compared against genealogy databases to find biological relatives, often distant ones. In Jacob's case, that comparison surfaced a relative of the infant's father. Genealogists then combined that genetic link with public records to work down the family tree until the parents could be named. (New to how consumer DNA and cousin-matching work in the first place? See our fascination-first guide, How DNA Remembers. For the full step-by-step, see our explainer on how forensic genetic genealogy actually works, and on how a DNA lab turns evidence into a lead.)

Two things about that process are worth holding onto, because they are the whole point of doing it carefully:

  • A genealogy match is a lead, not proof. It tells investigators where to look, not who is guilty. The identification of a person still has to be confirmed by conventional DNA comparison, and guilt is a separate question decided by a court, not a family tree. (We unpack exactly that line in is FGG evidence, or just an investigative lead?, and how it differs from the criminal DNA database in how CODIS differs from forensic genetic genealogy.)
  • The rules are narrow and written down. At the federal level, a genetic association is to be used "only as an investigative lead," and no one is to be arrested on that association alone — the framework we cover in what the DOJ rules actually require.

In this Neural Edge Publishing case file, Cassian Creed keeps the genetic-genealogy result in its proper evidentiary place: it produced a family lead, not a finding of guilt, and the criminal allegations still must be tested through conventional evidence and due process. That same restraint protects both Jacob Hope’s restored identity and Jennifer Lebron’s presumption of innocence.

Why the "lead, not proof" rule matters here

This case carries its own quiet argument for restraint. Back in 2001, a different woman was charged with first-degree murder in connection with Jacob's death — and those charges were later dropped. Someone was once accused in this case and was not the person the state ultimately chose to charge.

That is exactly why the modern standard insists a genetic match is only a starting point: the discipline of confirming a lead, gathering non-genetic evidence, and letting a court decide is what protects the people who are not guilty. It is also why the presumption of innocence applies now, fully, to Jennifer Lebron. An arrest is an allegation. A charge is not a verdict.

Restoring an identity

The most human part of this is the simplest. For twenty-three years a child was a case number. The science did not just generate a lead for prosecutors; it made it possible to say who he was, and to whom he belonged. Advocates named him Jacob Hope so he would be remembered as a person. That impulse — to return a name to someone who was reduced to an unknown — is the same one behind every genealogy identification, from recent cold cases to remains centuries old.

Readers following our coverage will recognize the pattern from another infant-Doe cold case we've documented: the Baby Boy Doe case file — Mansfield, 1985, a Massachusetts newborn known only as "Baby Boy Doe" for four decades until forensic genetic genealogy reopened the case in 2024. About

How we tell these stories

Cassian Creed publishes true-crime case files for readers who want to understand what actually happened — and what these cases teach about staying safe. Every account is built on the public record: court filings, verdicts, and contemporaneous reporting.

Who writes Cassian Creed

Cassian Creed is the author byline of Neural Edge Publishing, an independent true-crime imprint. The work is investigative in spirit: read the record, name the victims first, separate what is proven from what is still disputed, and explain it plainly. The focus is never the notoriety of a perpetrator — it is the people harmed and the lessons that help readers stay safe.

How these case files are made

Every claim is tied to a primary source — court documents, official records, and contemporaneous reporting. The research is AI-assisted and the editorial judgment is overseen by humans: each piece is checked against the record, weighed for victim dignity, and held to a consistent quality and accessibility standard before it is published. Where a case is still moving through the courts, we say so plainly; when we get something wrong, we correct it.

How our forensic analysis works — and its limits

Some case files include an independent forensic lens: our own read of the behavioral patterns, timeline, and evidence, powered by an analytical system we call A.I. AL and overseen by humans. We are transparent about how it works. Our analysis is "Internet Agile" — it is built entirely from the public record and publicly accessible sources: court filings, official statements, verified news reporting, and public databases. We do not have access to police case files, sealed evidence, or anything non-public, and we never pretend otherwise.

That is a deliberate strength and an honest limit at once. Working only from public information keeps our analysis independent and, in principle, checkable — but it also means our read can be incomplete. So we flag uncertainty, show our confidence honestly instead of dressing a guess as a fact, and treat our analysis as a lens for understanding, never a verdict. The real investigation belongs to law enforcement, not to us. We are grateful to the detectives, forensic scientists, and officers who do the hard, often thankless work of justice — and if you have information about a case, the right move is always to contact law enforcement directly, never us.

Our standard

We lead with the victims, not the perpetrators. We do not glamorize violence or trade in gratuitous detail. We name the people at the center of each case in life first. Where a verdict is under appeal, that is stated, not buried.

Corrections & sources

When we get something wrong, we fix it and say so. Spotted an error or have a correction? The preferred and fastest way to reach us is a public reply or mention on X at @CassianCreed. We monitor that account closely and review corrections against the public record. Corrections are made promptly and noted on the page. We never ask the public to send us crime tips or evidence; if you have information about a crime, contact law enforcement directly.

Why it matters

The point of a case file is not fear. It is clarity — and, where there is one, a safety lesson worth carrying. That is the promise behind every story here.

Reaching us

The fastest way to reach us is on X. Public replies or mentions to @CassianCreed are the preferred and quickest way to contact us, and we monitor that account closely.
